angle: 10 employees with 10 audiences beat one founder with one. What I saw at Ramp
linkedin_post:
10 audiences beat one founder's audience.

I saw this play out firsthand, and it changed how I think about reach.

If I have an audience, that's great. But if 10 people at our company each have their own independent audience, the reach we get is a huge amount bigger.

It shows up most around fundraise announcements. We get the whole team posting their own unique stories, and we coach people on how to do that well. It makes a world of difference.

I saw the same thing at Ramp in 2020 and 2021. X was the platform that worked there, and there was a lot of Twitter talk.

The people with the presence were mostly the early hires on the team. It was less about the founder.

A founder's voice is one channel. A team of people with their own stories is a network.

Who on your team should be posting but isn't?

Slide 2: Ten teammates with their own audiences multiply your reach.
Slide 3: We saw it most clearly on fundraise announcements.
Slide 4: Everyone posted their own unique story, not a copy-paste.
Slide 5: We coach people on how to post effectively.

Slide 8: Stop relying on one voice. Build a network of them.

lesson.title: Distribution comes from many voices, not one founder
takeaways: Ten people with independent audiences give you far more reach than one founder alone.
Big announcements like fundraises work best when the whole team posts their own unique stories.
At Ramp, early hires were often the ones with the strongest presence on X, not the founders.
lesson.exercise: Before your next company announcement, ask 5 teammates to each write a post from their own angle, and spend 15 minutes coaching each one on their story.

angle: The Dreamforce stunt drove fewer demos than the LinkedIn post about it
post_first_line: The Dreamforce post beat the Dreamforce stunt.
linkedin_post:
The Dreamforce post beat the Dreamforce stunt.

Not by a little. The LinkedIn post booked more demos than the in-person thing, by quite a bit.

We did an in real life stunt at Dreamforce a few months back. Before that, we got signs in the background of First Take leading up to the Super Bowl.

Some of these work in person. We definitely have cases of that. Some don't.

But the stunt isn't only the event. It's the raw material for the social post.

With AI lowering the barrier to entry for content, anyone can crank out words. Almost no one can fake something that happened in the real world.

So do the thing IRL, then translate it to social.

The other part I like: both of these came organically from our team. Nobody handed us a campaign brief. Being outside the box and doing something a little different is just fun.

What's your best IRL moment turned into content?

Slide 2: Not by a little. By quite a bit.
Slide 3: AI made written content cheap to produce.
Slide 4: Real-world moments are hard to fake.
Slide 5: Some stunts work in person. Some don't.
Slide 6: The social post can win even when the stunt doesn't.
Slide 7: Our best ideas came organically from the team.
Slide 8: Do it IRL, then translate it to social.

lesson.title: The stunt is the raw material, not the result
takeaways: AI lowers the barrier to creating content, so real-world moments stand out more.
An in-person stunt may not convert on site, but the social post about it can drive more demos.
Ideas that come organically from your team are worth acting on.
lesson.exercise: Pick one real-world thing your team can do this month, even something small. Plan how you'll capture it and post about it before you do it.

angle: The first LinkedIn post to write for any founder: your origin story
post_first_line: Founder origin stories consistently top the charts.
linkedin_post:
Founder origin stories consistently top the charts.

Tommy Clark says one post format keeps winning across all the clients the team works with.

It's the story behind the start of your company. Austin has posted a few versions of it on LinkedIn, including one just a couple weeks back.

Tommy Clark explains why it's always where the team starts: people just want to hear the story behind your company.

It works because it hits a few checkboxes at once:

It's a milestone announcement, and people like to celebrate you.

It humanizes you.

It's a story only you can tell.

And if there's conflict or an interesting moment in the founding story, which Tommy Clark says almost every founder has, the post gets even stronger.

What's the most interesting moment in your founding story?

angle: The simple monthly update post: one metric, 3 wins, 3 learnings, what's next
post_first_line: Tommy Clark breaks down the monthly update post.
linkedin_post:
Tommy Clark breaks down the monthly update post.

The structure is simple enough that most founders skip right past why it works.

It starts with one growth metric or exciting moment from the past month. Tommy Clark points to a percentage grown, a revenue milestone, a big logo landed, or a few key hires. Anything that catches attention on the timeline.

The more specific the metric, the better. Tommy Clark notes that these posts work well for Austin because Austin is okay sharing specific numbers.

After the hook, the post has 3 parts: 3 key highlights, 3 learnings from the past month, and what's next.

It's also much easier to execute than an origin story post. There's no narrative through line to build. It's just a highlight, a list of 3 wins, and what you learned.

Which metric would you lead with this month?

Slide 2: Start with one metric or exciting moment from the month
Slide 3: Growth percentage, revenue milestone, big logo, or key hires
Slide 4: The more specific the metric, the better the hook
Slide 5: Then share 3 key highlights from the past month
Slide 6: Add 3 learnings from the past month
Slide 7: Close with what's next
Slide 8: No narrative through line needed, easier than an origin story

lesson.title: The Monthly Update Post Formula
takeaways: Lead with one specific growth metric or exciting event from the past month.
Follow the hook with 3 highlights, 3 learnings, and what's next.
It's easier to write than an origin story because it needs no narrative through line.
lesson.exercise: Write down your single most attention-grabbing metric or milestone from the last month, make it as specific as you can, then list 3 wins, 3 learnings, and what's next.

angle: LinkedIn content has asymmetric upside, but stop asking 'content or outbound' and stack both.
post_first_line: Tens of demos booked per month from content.
linkedin_post:
Tens of demos booked per month from content.

That's the upside nobody budgets for.

Content has asymmetric upside. If you're good at it, it can be the best-returning thing you do. It doesn't take that much time, either.

That's been our own lived experience at Unify. But it's a bit of a standout case.

So I don't think the real question is content or outbound.

My belief is that a pipeline strategy should be multichannel. Think less about this or that, and more about how you keep stacking wins.

Outbound and outreach on LinkedIn is one win. Content on LinkedIn is another.

Stack them. Don't pick one.

Which channel are you underinvesting in right now?

lesson.title: Stack channels instead of choosing one
takeaways: Content has asymmetric upside: if you're good at it, it can be the best-returning thing you do.
Our results at Unify are a standout case, so don't assume they're guaranteed.
A pipeline strategy should be multichannel. Think about stacking wins, not this or that.
lesson.exercise: List every channel generating pipeline for you today. Mark each as running or not, then pick one missing win, like LinkedIn content or LinkedIn outreach, and add it this month.

angle: AI made posting easy. Here's why that makes your stories the only thing worth posting
post_first_line: Tommy Clark: posting on LinkedIn just got easy.
linkedin_post:
Tommy Clark: posting on LinkedIn just got easy.

That changes what's worth posting.

Anyone can toss a prompt into Claude or ChatGPT and get a pretty okay piece of LinkedIn copy. The timeline is getting more crowded as a result.

So Tommy's advice is to create content AI can't copy.

One way to do that: shift from how-to, value-oriented content to how-Tommy-did-it content. More narrative. More stories.

The rule Tommy likes to use: pair every single take with a story.

A take on its own is easy to generate. A story only the author can tell is not.

What story could you pair with your next take?

lesson.title: Pair every take with a story
takeaways: AI lowered the barrier to posting, so the timeline is more crowded.
Shifting from how-to content to how-I content helps you stand out.
Pairing every take with a story creates content AI can't copy.
